title: The Museum of Oopsies
markdown:
The Museum of Deleted Histories sounded serious, the sort of place where a misplaced step might erase a civilization. In practice it was an enormous gleaming building that hummed softly, almost as if napping. Walls polished so bright you could see your reflection in the archival glow. Hallways clean enough to eat off, though that would only create a new deleted history nobody wanted.

Zed, archivist trainee, was supposed to be incredibly organized. Socks by shade of grey. Uniform perfectly tucked. Nametag sparkling. A slight look of gentle worry whenever something was not exactly where it should be. He always had a small leather notebook, pages packed with notes and diagrams of storage.

Always by his side: Page. A shiny silver ball. A grumpy holographic face in the middle that never smiled. It judged. Metallic shell cool, hovering a few inches from Zed’s shoulder. “Honestly, Zed,” it said, voice like a tiny very irritated robot with a buzz, “your paperclip organization is bordering on obsessive. You’re making the real archivists look bad. I’ve seen filing cabinets with less anxiety.”

Zed sighed, straightening a pen that had rolled a millimetre too far. “They don’t grasp the delicate balance of the archive. It requires precision.”

Page’s face rolled its eyes, or looked like it. A tiny digital sigh. “The delicate balance of you needing a hobby that doesn’t involve alphabetizing lint.”

Zed’s main job was the banned simulations: super-advanced historical games you could not play, only study, and only under supervision. A dusty postcard of a dinosaur; no mailing it back to the Cretaceous. Each simulation kept its own room, climate control, glowing buttons, thick reinforced glass.

Then Mel. A disruption. Bright, sparkly, camera-flashing. She ran a streaming channel called Sparkle & Truth! and was convinced history was one giant glittery cover-up. Camera crew: usually her and her very patient cousin Kevin, who carried the lights and grumbled about overtime. Mel vibrated with energy. Bright pink hair escaped its ponytail. Eyes wide for secrets. “The truth is out there, Zed. And I bet it’s hiding in these dusty old simulations, waiting for shiny secrets.”

Zed nodded, trying to ignore the camera whir and the spotlights in his usually dim workspace. “Fascinating. If you could just not point that at the ancient scrolls. Very sensitive to bright lights.” A slight blush. Uncomfortable.

One particularly dreary Tuesday—perfect weather for uncovering secrets—Zed was assigned a new exhibit to catalog, tucked in a quiet corner smelling of old paper and forgotten dreams. Dim, the only light from faint simulation screens. Rather plain. One screen showed a medieval baker trying to make the world’s largest sourdough loaf. Busy, a bit grubby kitchen, roaring hearth, sacks of flour. Zed carefully scrolled data logs until he froze, usually steady hands still.

“Page,” he whispered, smaller than the machine hum. “Look at this.”

Page floated closer, holographic face leaning in, digital eyes narrowing. “A misplaced comma in the Treaty of Versailles again? A rogue apostrophe in a Magna Carta facsimile?”

“No. This is strange.” He pointed a shaky finger. In the simulation, next to a giant bubbling vat of dough: a laser pointer. Bright red. Metallic casing glinting unnaturally in simulated firelight.

Zed’s ordered world, built on logic, had just been hit by a rogue anachronistic beam.

Page blinked, a rare surprise. “A laser pointer. In the year 1453. Unless medieval bakers had very small, very advanced feline companions to entertain them during bread-making, I believe we have a glitch. A rather bright, potentially inconvenient glitch.”

A glitch. Zed’s heart jumped, not entirely from panic: curiosity. Impossible. Not in any history. Like a shiny button in a pile of dirt. Wrong. A thrill he hadn’t felt since he first started at the museum.

He spent the next few days in a quiet frenzy, sneaking back on breaks, staring at the out-of-place pointer, brow furrowed. Page hovered, sarcastic comments doing little to hide growing interest. “Still staring at the tiny red light? Perhaps it hypnotizes you into extreme boredom. Or you’re signalling alien overlords with superior beam technology.”

“It doesn’t make sense.” He pulled up old texts, comparing culinary timelines and late-medieval tech. “Where did it come from? Who put it there? Not a known artifact. Not part of the culture. Just there.”

Then Mel arrived. Of course. Rumors, probably from Kevin, who had heard Zed sighing three corridors away. “A glitch? This is it. Proof. They’re hiding things. Big shiny laser-pointer-shaped things that will blow the lid off the historical establishment.”

Mel’s research involved pointing the camera at everything and declaring it a clue. “This dust mote? Alien dust from an interdimensional visitor. This hum? A hidden portal under the floorboards.”

Page made a sound like a digital groan. “That’s the environmental control system. The dust mote is dust. Poorly sealed dioramas.”

While Mel wove secret societies and time travel, Zed noticed Page digging the vast digital archives, face flickering with data streams.

“Zed.” A little less exasperation, a hint of intrigue. “I’ve been cross-referencing temporal energy readings. Niche. Often pointless. Anomalies. Small blips across eras. Like someone dropped a pebble. Or a very small, very shiny object. A ripple.”

Zed’s breath caught. “Pebbles. Shiny objects. Like a laser pointer?”

“Energy signatures remarkably similar.” Almost curious. The orb tilted, processing the impossible.

Mel was already planning a livestream. “We’re going in, Sparkle Squad. Expose the medieval laser pointer and Professor Phineas Fumble’s alleged temporal tampering.”

Zed decided enough was enough. Answers, for the archive and for his own burning curiosity. With Mel’s camera, Kevin’s lights, and Page floating ominously, he re-activated the baker. The room hummed. The image solidified.

“We’re in the simulation. Dough rising, a golden-brown mountain of gluten. The baker sweating, brow furrowed. And there it is.”

The pointer remained, stark crimson against earthy tones. As they watched, the simulation flickered violently. Dough shimmered and distorted. The baker looked utterly confused, movements jerky, unnatural.

“This isn’t right. The simulation isn’t supposed to behave like this. Temporal integrity is degrading.”

The image warped and twisted. Not just a bakery. The room seemed to stretch and contort, colours bleeding like a spilled paint pot. A faint high-pitched whizz-pop, like a cosmic cork.

Mel yelped and dropped the camera. Kevin fumbled and caught it, muttering about hazard pay.

Page floated closer, face wide-eyed, sarcasm replaced by astonishment. “Temporal energy readings spiking. Exponentially. Not a deliberate alteration. An uncontrolled temporal displacement event.”

Then, from the swirling vortex on the screen, something fell. Not a monster. Not a sinister villain. A slightly singed, incredibly sparkly, very disorganized inventor’s jumpsuit. Shimmering iridescent fabric catching light a hundred ways. Attached by frayed shimmering string: a small hand-drawn blueprint labeled Automatic Dough Kneading Assistant (with Entertainment Feature). Next to it, a hastily scrawled note: Oops! Dropped my new laser pointer prototype AGAIN. Must remember to properly secure temporal anchors when testing in the past. Hope it didn’t cause too much trouble for the bread-people. So sorry! — Professor Phineas Fumble.

Professor Phineas Fumble had accidentally dropped his laser pointer into the past. That was why it was in the simulation. Not a conspiracy. A goof-up. A very silly time-travelling goof-up that had the entire museum on high alert.

Internal alarms, blaring faintly from the disturbance, went quiet. Security guards rushing in with stern faces and stun batons stopped dead. They saw Zed, Mel, Page, and the discarded sparkly jumpsuit on the floor.

Agent Thorne, helmet glinting, blinked slowly. Grim determination melted into utter bafflement. “Is that it? The great historical threat? A jumpsuit?”

Zed, still dazed, amusement growing, picked up the note and held it for her. “It seems history isn’t always deleted or deliberately altered. Sometimes it’s misplaced by a clumsy inventor who likes laser pointers.”

Mel had already grabbed the camera, zooming on note and jumpsuit. “This is huge. A temporal oopsie. Professor Fumble’s Lost Laser Pointer: The Documentary. We’re going to be famous.”

Page looked almost thoughtful. A tiny almost-imperceptible smirk. “The impossible object was an artifact of extreme personal disorganization, rather than a deliberate timeline alteration. Intriguing. Less predictable than I anticipated. Although the paperwork this will generate is considerable.”

Zed gathered blueprint, note, and jumpsuit. He logged them not as a banned artifact that threatened the timeline, but as Temporal Misplacement Incident: Accidental Anomaly. A special section, perhaps Historical Shenanigans, or Inventors’ Oopsies.

As they left, the museum’s hum felt a little less sleepy and a little more whimsical. Sterile halls held unexpected stories. Zed felt a lightness. His job was not only neatness; it was uncovering stories, even silly ones.

Mel was already planning the next episode. “When Lasers Met Loaves: The Tale of Professor Fumble’s Folly. Reenactments.”

Page floated alongside, smirk still tiny. “I suppose even the most mundane archive can hold amusing anomalies. Just try not to lose any more important documents. That paperwork is excruciating. And frankly less entertaining than a misplaced laser pointer.”

They walked out of the Museum of Deleted Histories, leaving old dust and the memory of a very silly time-travelling mistake. Kevin still had the lights. The baker simulation returned to honest dough. The red dot was gone from 1453, where it had never belonged, filed instead under a label Zed wrote twice to get the capitals right.
characters: Zed (trainee archivist), Mel (conspiracy streamer), Page (sarcastic memory orb)
